title: Field trip dedicated to the life and contributions of Dr. Martin Lockley to understanding Front Range Geology and Paleontology: Selected Special Metropolitan Denver, Colorado area World Class Geologic Heritage Sites
chairs: Tim Connors
description: This trip will visit a selected suite of world class Geologic Heritage sites easily viewable in a single day field trip including: Red Rocks Park Amphitheatre NHL (National Historic Landmark), Morrison-Golden Fossil Areas NNL (National Natural Landmarks (aka. Dinosaur Ridge, Fossil Trace Golf Course / Triceratops Trail), Jurassic Morrison Formation type section, Interstate 70 Roadcut, Table Mountain Lava Flows, and Uranium roll front (Colorado Highway 470 & US 285). Dr. Martin Lockley was instrumental in the elevation of the Morrison Fossil Area NNL to add other sites and to expand to the Morrison-Golden Fossil Areas NNL in 2011. Field guides will be supplied, as well as numerous online resources related to each of the visited sites. Local NPS, USGS and academic geologists will “tag-team” to discuss the viewed geologic features, issues and processes. Rocks, fossils, mineral deposits, landforms, and structural features of varying ages from Precambrian to Cenozoic are present from the “Great Unconformity” of Precambrian rocks overlain by Pennsylvanian Fountain Formation at Red Rocks Park; to great sections of Paleozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic rocks of variable types and structural orientations. As part of the stop involving Dinosaur Ridge, there will be a visit to the “Martin G. Lockley Discovery Center” to view the “Deep Time Detour” exhibits and building that are a living tribute to his legacy in promoting geologic and paleontologic heritage in Colorado’s Front Range for whom this field trip is dedicated. This trip will have sponsorship from the Friends of Dinosaur Ridge and Colorado Scientific Society.

title: Quantitative analysis, visualization, and modelling of detrital geochronology data
chairs: Joel Saylor, Kurt Sundell, Glenn Sharman, Ryan Nielsen, Chance Ronemus
description: Alongside the growth in detrital geochronology datasets is a developing body of best practices, techniques, and tools for analyzing these data. This course will introduce participants to the technical background necessary to understand and apply recently developed sample comparison and data analysis techniques, including quantitative intersample comparison, data visualization, and mixture modelling. Following a theoretical and hands-on introduction, we will apply existing tools for the expedited analysis of large datasets. This introduction will familiarize users with working in Python and Matlab, but no coding experience is necessary to participate. Participants are encouraged to bring their own datasets, if available.

title: New insights into the Ancestral Rocky Mountain and Laramide orogenies, Oligocene magmatism and metamorphism, and Rio Grande rift extension along the western flank of the Sangre de Cristo Range, Colorado
chairs: John Singleton Samantha Malavarca, Michelle Gevedon
description: This 3-day, 2-night field trip examines the complex geologic history of the Sangre de Cristo Range near Great Sand Dunes National Park and Crestone, Colorado, emphasizing new research that provides key insight into the region’s tectonic evolution. The Sangre de Cristo Range exposes some of the deepest Cenozoic structural levels in the Rocky Mountain region and is critical for understanding how multiple orogenic events and geologic structures relate to one another. Field trip stops include short (<0.5 mile) to moderate (~3 mile) hikes to outcrops associated with the Pennsylvanian–Permian Ancestral Rocky Mountains, the Late Cretaceous–early Paleogene Laramide orogeny, Oligocene intrusive magmatism and contact metamorphism, and Rio Grande rift extension. Highlights include exposures of brittle-plastic deformation along the Mosca Creek thrust and evidence for an early Oligocene pulse of ENE-directed shortening; examples of the (likely) highest-grade metamorphism of Phanerozoic strata in the Rocky Mountain region; mylonitic fabrics recording thrust- and normal-sense shear along the Independence Mine shear zone; Quaternary fault scarps up to ~10 m high; and the tallest sand dunes in North America. Discussion topics will address structural reactivation; relationships between contractional and extensional structures; the transition from Laramide shortening to Rio Grande rift extension; links between Oligocene magmatism and deformation; and the impact of deglaciation on late Pleistocene to Holocene fault slip. Participants will stay in dormitory-style lodging at Colorado College’s Baca Campus near Crestone, with evening presentations and access to petrographic microscopes for thin sections from field stops.

title: Fourmile Creek: Exploring mountain watershed dynamics from Pikes Peak to Canon City
chairs: Randy Stotler, Marcia Schulmeister
description: Water resources in the mountain west are stressed, with reduced snowfall, increasing population, and persistent water quality issues. The Fourmile Creek watershed stretches from the top of Colorado’s front range to arid canyons before it exits to the plains, and provides an excellent opportunity to examine these issues. The field trip will explore the evolution of Fourmile Creek, from its Pike’s Peak headwaters, to its confluence with the Arkansas River. We will investigate headwater dynamics along part of the Gold Belt Scenic Byway in the Cripple Creek and Victor mining district and explore the legacy of historic underground and modern open pit/heap leach mining. Where Cripple Creek joins Fourmile Creek and enters canyon country, we will the assess neutral mine drainage effects on water quality and quantity. We’ll travel along the historic and steep Shelf Road wagon supply route and visit exotic streams, phreatophytes, irrigation, and examine the fate of mining- derived and geogenic chemical constituents in surface water and groundwater. Downstream stops will feature academic, cultural, and historic points of interest, such as the University of Kansas Harrison Field Station, markers of early explorers, and the Garden Park fossil area, which is known for the classic bone wars of the late 19th century. The trip ends at the Arkansas River in Canon City, with an optional dinner stop at a local Canon City brew pub.

title: Friable Fins, Fizzy Water, Fragile Fossils, and Fine Gold: A Geologic Sampler of the Pikes Peak Region
chairs: Barbara EchoHawk, Uwe Richard Kackstaetter
description: Join us for an unforgettable one-day field trip through the breathtaking Pikes Peak region. This whirlwind tour visits four iconic geologic sites, each with its own fascinating story. Our first stop is majestic Garden of the Gods, where stunning vertical fins of orange and cream sandstone tower overhead. Next is charming Manitou Springs and the eight cold springs that bubble to the surface with effervescent, potable mineral waters. Then it’s on to Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument and its collection of delicate, remarkably preserved insect and floral fossils, as well as its petrified, lahar-battered sequoia stumps. Our last stop is the historic Cripple Creek Mining District, where gold fever is still contagious. Geoscientists and every participant of any age who is curious about the natural world are welcome on this field trip. As we stroll through each site, we’ll engage in discussions that link the local geology to broader regional and geohistorical contexts. Between stops, the gorgeous vistas of the Pikes Peak massif and Southern Front Range are sure to spark inspiration for your future geological explorations. With topics guided by participant interests, our discussions may expand into captivating areas such as Paleozoic stratigraphy, Laramide structure, low-temperature aqueous geochemistry, Cenozoic volcanism and climate, alkaline diatreme complexes, hydrothermal alteration, mining gold tellurides, and more. Come share this opportunity to connect with fellow enthusiasts and deepen your understanding of the planet’s geological wonders. Join us for a day of discovery, learning, and connection to this little corner of our amazing Earth.

title: Compiling digital stratigraphic models for sedimentary geochemistry, Earth history, and paleobiology
chairs: Erik Sperling, Daven Quinn, Shanan Peters, Una Farrell
description: This workshop will prepare participants to contribute stratigraphic and sedimentary geochemistry data into the linked infrastructure of the Macrostrat and Sedimentary Geochemistry and Paleoenvironments (SGP) databases. We will overview the design, collaboration structure, and scientific motivation of these projects, emerging community curation approaches, and data synthesis efforts focused on high-resolution stratigraphy associated with sedimentary geochemical data. Workshop participants will learn how to find data in these databases and how to format their data for inclusion. Participants will have the opportunity to propose targets for digitization, join working groups for data-driven science, and provide feedback on workflows and future development.

title: Introduction to luminescence and electron spin resonance dating and thermochronology techniques
chairs: Nathan Brown, Kathleen Rodrigues, Caleb K. Walcott-George
description: Luminescence and electron spin resonance techniques (together known as trapped charge methods), are rapidly evolving, with applications in Quaternary geology, geomorphology, active tectonics, thermochronology, geoarchaeology, and radiation dosimetry. This short course is designed for students, researchers, and industry professionals interested in applying these techniques to geological, physical, and archaeological problems. The course introduces the fundamental scientific principles underlying trapped-charge methods, outlines best practices for sample collection and preparation, and discusses emerging and future applications. Through selected case studies, the course will highlight a wide range of archaeological and geological applications and provide guidance on integrating these methods into research.

title: StraboField – Learning about digital collection of field data by doing it.
chairs: Doug Walker Claire Martin
description: This trip will give participants hands-on instruction and practice using the StraboField mobile app. The app and underlying vocabulary were developed with community input across the geosciences. Besides research efforts, using StraboField is percolating into many field courses. Its interface is designed to help users collect complete and logically consistent datasets. It offers several features especially suited to instruction in field courses, including a notebook view of student work and easily digested maps and field information. Data from structural geology, petrology, sedimentology/stratigraphy, and earthquake reporting are supported. Days will be in the field, with evening sessions to understand the data system, how to robustly save and duplicate data, and how to adapt usage to field exercises for students. The trip will go to Cañon City, Colorado, to visit outcrop and mapping areas used by the KU Geology and many other schools. Target geology includes a monocline developed in Paleozoic rocks, thrust-faulted Ordovician strata, and amphibolite-grade and folded quartzite, schist, and gneiss. We anticipate three field days spanning October 15 to 17. We will depart from Denver on the evening of October 14, and participants can leave the trip starting at 4 pm on 10/17. StraboField was developed with NSF funding. It is free to download, use, and upload to a cloud server. Data are accessible at the interface https://strabospot.org/ . The app runs on both iOS and Android, and is compatible with most phones and tablets. YouTube videos are available at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC-bWoOvRvpedOswFERXQPiw .

title: Methods and Geological Applications in Geo-Thermo-Petro-Chronology I
chairs: Mauricio Ibanez-Mejia | Department of Geosciences, Michelle Foley, Martin Senger, Manuela Botero
description: Day 1 of this course will focus on chemical systems and geologic questions commonly interrogated by Laser Ablation Inductively Coupled Plasma–Mass Spectrometry analysis of minerals including U-Th-Pb, Lu-Hf, and trace elements, with an emphasis on geochronology and petrochronology of zircon. Day 1 will be divided in various modules, each consisting of a first half that will be lecture-based and focus on theory, while the second half will be hands-on data interpretation using spreadsheet-based exercises and open-source software tools for data analysis and visualization. This course is geared toward geoscience faculty, professional scientists, graduate students, and undergraduate students.

title: Proterozoic Metamorphism and Deformation of the Colorado Front Range: Crustal assembly to intracontinental reworking
chairs: Ian Hillenbrand Amy Gilmer, Alexander Lusk
description: The Proterozoic rocks of Colorado's Front Range are a world-class example of accretionary orogenesis and subsequent intracontinental reworking. This one-day pre-meeting trip will examine key exposures that record nearly a billion years of tectonic history, from Paleoproterozoic arc accretion through Mesoproterozoic magmatism and deformation. Purpose: Participants will explore the evidence for multiple tectonometamorphic events preserved in Front Range rocks and discuss how recent advances in petrochronology and tectonic modeling are reshaping our understanding of Proterozoic crustal assembly. The trip provides field context for the companion technical session "Proterozoic Tectonics of Western Laurentia." Itinerary: Departing Denver at 8:00 AM (7 am?), we will visit four stops in the Front Range west of the city. Stops will highlight Paleoproterozoic metasedimentary and metavolcanic rocks, fabrics and mineral assemblages associated with ca. 1.7 and 1.4 Ga deformation and metamorphism as well as shear zones recording polyphase deformation. We will return to Denver by approximately 6:00 PM . The trip is designed to be accessible to participants at all career stages, including students, with introductory discussions at each stop to provide context for the complex geologic history. Leaders will provide a field guide for use during the trip.

title: Practical Geoconservation: Global Perspectives on the Protection and Promotion of Geological Sites
chairs: Jack James Matthews, Sherene James-Williamson, Maria da Glória Garcia, Manu R. Monge-Ganuzas
description: Have you ever wondered what you can do to help conserve and celebrate an important geological site? Our planet’s geosites may be recognised for their scientific, educational, aesthetics, or cultural significance, and can range from private sites, to local nature reserves, to UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Led by a team of international experts, this course will include presentations and discussions on topics including conservation interventions, geoheritage management, monitoring, interpretation, and community engagement. Using examples from around the world, we will focus on practical geoconservation actions that will assist both beginners and experts to protect and promote sites of geological significance.

title: Diachronous exhumation on Colorado's High Plains and Rocky Mountains
chairs: Lon D. Abbott, Sabrina Kainz Taran Renfrow, James R. Metcalf, Rebecca M. Flowers
description: On this three-day trip we’ll visit locations in Colorado’s High Plains and Rocky Mountains, including the iconic Spanish Peaks and spectacular Crested Butte areas, that experienced exhumation at different times during the Cenozoic, as revealed by low-temperature thermochronometry. Miocene kilometer-scale exhumation occurred on Colorado’s southeastern High Plains, but the northeastern plains were unaffected. The Rockies tell a similar tale. The last significant exhumation affecting much of the range occurred in the Eocene, but a 120-km-diameter patch of land between Glenwood Springs and Gunnison exhumed 3-4 km during the Miocene. We’ll examine the evidence for diachronous exhumation and contemplate its implications. Colorado’s surface uplift history is especially puzzling; one primary use of the exhumation history is to test competing hypotheses for the anomalously high elevation of both the Colorado Rockies and High Plains. We’ll compare the timing and spatial patterns of surface uplift predicted by the various hypotheses with Colorado’s exhumation history to winnow viable hypotheses from the unviable. This trip, co-led by young scientists whose undergraduate research helped reveal the diachronous exhumation, will visit Boulder and the Spanish Peaks on Day 1 to contrast northeastern and southeastern High Plains exhumation histories. We’ll stay in lovely La Veta, leaving time for those interested to discuss local geoheritage initiatives. On Day 2, we’ll explore Crested Butte’s grand scenery, examining a 120-km-diameter dome of Miocene exhumation, staying the night in Crested Butte. Day 3 sees us return to Denver, observing the record of Eocene Arkansas Hills exhumation, east of Salida, on the way.

title: StraboField and StraboMicro for Early Career Professionals
chairs: Doug Walker | Geology, Julie Newman | Geology, Basil Tikoff | Geology, Ellen Nelson | Geology
description: The StraboSpot database and applications enable geologic data collection, storage, and sharing across scales and disciplines. StraboField and StraboMicro are designed to help Geologists collect data and integrate field data with laboratory observations and associated data. Both are designed to integrate images seamlessly into the database. The data system was developed through community outreach workshops to establish vocabulary and data reporting standards. The short course aims to introduce early career scientists to StraboField and the StraboMicro application and help participants design and build projects for both research and teaching. The systems can be viewed at http://strabospot.org.

title: Sedimentary recycling of high-pressure rocks in subduction complex clastic rocks, including mélanges, and localization of subduction interface slip.
chairs: John Wakabayashi Ron Rubin, David Shimabukuro
description: This 3-day trip views mélange and coherent outcrops of the Franciscan Complex in Sonoma County, western California, that bear on the localization of subduction and exhumation slip, sedimentary mixing in mélanges, recycling of previously-subducted rocks, and multiscale architecture of the subduction complex. Many of the stops feature tourist-worthy scenery. We plan lodging in the Windsor-Healdsburg area. Coastal stops will include Jenner Beach, a fabulous pile of eclogite and garnet blueschist talus at the mouth of the Russian River, and north Shell Beach with exceptional exposures of mélange matrix showing its derivation from conglomerate and an incredible variety of blocks. Inland, we will see outcrops of the Skaggs Springs schist, a coherent quartz-rich blueschist unit, including an outcrop with internal blocks of blueschist-overprinted amphibolite and eclogite along the Old Skaggs Springs Road, serpentinite matrix mélange with embedded amphibolite and blueschist block and the New Skaggs Road. Near the latter we will view outcrops of gabbro/quartz diorite of the Coast Range ophiolite. Along the shoreline of Lake Sonoma, we will view blueschist facies imbricated ocean plate stratigraphy with associated fault rocks including apparent pseudotachylyte, as well as a >200 m garnet amphibolite block embedded in serpentinite matrix informally nicknamed "The Lord of the Blocks". Wine tasting at Dry Creek Vineyards and visits to craft breweries, such as Russian River Brewing Company are planned for those that wish to do so.

title: Deposition, magmatism, metamorphism, and deformation of the Proterozoic Poudre Basin in the northern Colorado Front Range
chairs: Graham Baird, Kevin Mahan Timothy Grover
description: Join us on a day-long field trip to see the Proterozoic igneous and metamorphic rocks of the Poudre Canyon and Big Thompson Canyon area in the northern Colorado Front Range. We’ll see a wide variety of lithologies, including quartzite, schist, amphibolite, and gneiss, as well as subduction related plutons and enigmatic beryl-bearing felsic pegmatites. Presented geochemistry, geochronology, and metamorphic petrology datasets will connect these rocks to various tectonic models explaining their origins and the regional implications for crust generation and Proterozoic tectonics. Cost will include roundtrip transportation from the convention center and lunch.

title: Ai Tools and Databases for Geoscience
chairs: James G Ogg, Grant M Boquet | GeoGPT, Yitian Xiao, Michael Stephenson
description: AI-assistants and interlinked databases are powerful tools for research and education in geoscience. The hands-on exercises in this short-course will explore a range such systems, including GeoGPT (Large Language models trained on geological material including your own uploaded library, geologic-map analysis and making, etc.), global database of geological formations with one-click display onto paleogeographic maps (geolex.org), taxonomy assistant and a comprehensive database of fossils (ca. 40,000 genera), generation of charts for all types of Earth history information, etc. The session will conclude with a discussion on AI-tools and the future of geoscientific research.

title: Methods and geological applications in geo-thermo-petro-chronology II
chairs: Mauricio Ibanez-Mejia | Department of Geosciences, Kendra Murray | Department of Geosciences, Leah E Morgan | United States Geological Survey
description: Part II of this short course will focus on methods and applications of diffusion-based thermochronology and petrochronology. Topics will include an introduction to diffusion, and thermo-petrochonologic applications of the (U-Th)/He, Ar/Ar, Sm-Nd, and U-Pb systems. Topics will incorporate a mix of theory, application, and hands-on activities. This course is geared toward any geoscientist wanting to learn about these topics, including faculty, professional scientists, graduate students, and undergraduate students.

title: Preserving Geology: Advanced Digital Outcrop Modeling and Interpretation
chairs: William Brown Hawkins | Pix4D, David Hodgetts | VRGeoscience Limited, Brian S Burnham | VRGeoscience Limited
description: Digital outcrop models support both academic research and industry workflows in structural geology, sedimentology and geotechnical analysis. Advances in photogrammetric reconstruction facilitate generation of large, high-resolution 3D outcrop models, yet texture resampling and compression often reduce image clarity and obscure fine scale geological features. This workshop demonstrates how to process and use Pix4Dmatic outputs and the Open Photogrammetry Format, OPF, within VRGS to preserve image fidelity during interpretation. Participants link measurements and annotations to source imagery while maintaining full three-dimensional context. This integrated workflow strengthens reproducibility, improves interpretive confidence, and supports rigorous digital outcrop characterisation in research and applied settings.

title: Analyzing the Nation’s geology with the Cooperative National Geologic Map
chairs: Sam Johnstone | U.S. Geological Survey, Joe Colgan | U.S. Geological Survey
description: In Fall of 2025 the USGS released the Cooperative National Geologic Map; a resource that integrates and synthesizes maps from around the country into a consistent representation of the Nation’s geology at and beneath the Earth’s surface. This course will introduce participants to the philosophy and processes used to construct the map and walk through some practical examples of extracting content from it. We will work with the map through the online interface, using GIS software, and delve into using Python to access and manipulate the synthesized maps and primary data contained within the database.

title: 'Denver's Urban Riverscapes: Improving Resilience, Improving Connections
chairs: Anne MacDonald David Skuodas
description: Urban settings are rife with hydrological and geomorphicological modification from land use changes, dams, and diversions. Increasingly, too, urban streams are seen as potential providers of robust ecosystem support. Just as the Denver metro area has grown over the past 30 years, so, too, has the regional interest in applying strategies for that can increase the resilience of urban stream corridors. Nature-based design in an urban setting must account for the the special roles of both hydrologic and community context. Successful outcomes in an urban setting must account for the hydrologic and geomorphic setting, which can be quite dynamic and also quite unnatural when compared to prehistory. Since we’re in the context of a city, designs that work well also strike a balance with neighborhood scale community values and the amount of space we have to work with. Applying our contextual understanding allows them to better function as refuges for humans and biota alike. This field trip will highlight some of these strategies found in the Denver metro area, addressing issues of: managing changes in runoff volume resulting from new development reducing or managing erosion and flooding hazards providing ecosystem services by enhancing aquatic and floodplain biota (including beaver re-introduction), and providing recreational opportunities within the urban area. We'll look at small creeks, range-front streams, and even the Platte River in central Denver, where a kayak course what installed in the mid-1980s that led to insights used in rehabilitating trout streams.

title: Landslide mapping using lidar and orthoimagery in a GIS – building fundamental mapping skills for the next generation of landslide scientists
chairs: Stephen L Slaughter, Matthew Crawford | University of Kentucky, William Burns
description: This short course teaches essential techniques for creating landslide inventories using lidar and orthoimagery. Inventories are critical for hazard assessments and decision-making by planners, land managers, insurers, transportation agencies, emergency managers, regulators, homeowners, academics, and geologic surveys. Accurate landslide mapping in GIS is a key geoscience skill. Through demonstrations and hands-on exercises, participants will map landslides and evaluate features across the U.S. Topics include mapping specific features, elevation change detection, pros and cons of automated mapping, and models for hazard maps such as runout and susceptibility analyses. Prior ArcGIS experience and basic landslide process knowledge are required.

title: Black Hills and Badlands: A Synopsis of Geological Time
chairs: Spencer Cody Jill Cody
description: Join us on an exciting three-day adventure in the Black Hills and Badlands of South Dakota on our GSA Denver Conference field trip. During those three days, we will cover a remarkable array of Earth's prehistory through highlighting the stunning rock formations of the Black Hills and Badlands paired with some of the most amazing paleontological finds in the world. On day one we will travel from Denver to the Northern Black Hills to explore the uplift that formed the Black Hills at Bear Butte, a stunning laccolith formation. We will continue our day by traveling back in time as we progress deeper into the Black Hills via Spearfish Canyon revealing the remarkable geological record preserved in sedimentary rock arriving in Lead at the Lead Dome complex to tour what was one of the world’s biggest producers of gold, the Homestake Gold Mine, while learning about the cutting-edge science currently being conducted in what is a world-class underground lab. The next day we will cover the remarkable pegmatite granite spires of the Needles in Custer State Park and pegmatite dike formations of Mount Rushmore National Monument. We will cover Karst topography and formations with a tour of Jewel Cave National Monument, the Mammoth Site, and Wind Cave National Park. Once we have finished our tours of Karst formations, we will make our way out onto the plains to learn about the sedimentary deposits and fossils of Badlands National Park. All admission fees, passes, meals, snacks, and hotel lodging are included!

title: Fundamentals and Geoscience Applications of Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry
chairs: John Cottle, Andrew Kylander-Clark, Morgan Adamson
description: This short course introduces the principles and applications of Time-of-Flight (ToF) Mass Spectrometry in earth and environmental sciences. As research addresses complex challenges in geochronology, petrology, hydrology, and forensics, the advantages of high-speed, full-spectrum mass analysis become increasingly significant. The program covers ToF separation physics and sample introduction systems, highlighting case studies in geochronology, trace metal analysis, aerosol characterization, and non-target environmental screening. Dedicated sessions focus on real-time data collection, processing workflows, and software tools for managing high-resolution datasets. Participants will gain the skills to design experiments, interpret complex data, and integrate ToF-MS into their research programs.

title: Inverting Bedrock River Profiles: Theory, Practice, and Applications
chairs: Sean F Gallen | Department of Geosciences, Frank J Pazzaglia | Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences
description: This one-day short course introduces theory and practical implementation of river-profile inversion methods used to infer uplift histories, base-level change, and landscape response to tectonic forcing. Participants will learn the conceptual basis of channel profile analysis and apply inversion techniques using MATLAB and the open-source TopoToolbox framework. Hands-on exercises will guide participants through data preparation, model assumptions, calibration and execution, uncertainty assessment, and interpretation of results. Participants may work with provided example datasets or optionally apply the methods to their own digital elevation models.

title: The Central City Gravel, Nussbaum Gravel, and Rocky Flats Alluvium: Stemming Over 100 Years of Research and Establishing 1.5 Million Years of Southern Rocky Mountain-Laurentide Geomorphology
chairs: Cal Ruleman, Marith Reheis Adam Hudson, William Odom , Ralph Shroba, Brent Goehring, Marc Caffee
description: Join us for a day trip exploring 1.5 million years of glacial and glaciofluvial history of Colorado’s Front Range, the Central Colorado Icefield as related to coeval maximum extents of the Laurentide Icesheet ~1.3 Ma, and formation of the South Platte, Missouri, and Arkansas Rivers. We will begin the trip by visiting the oldest known preserved glacial deposit within the Front Range, the ~1.4 Ma Central City Gravel, discussing how early 20 th century geologists, including Kirk Bryan, Wallace Atwood, and Glenn Scott, interpreted these regionally dispersed glacial deposits. We will also discuss the Central City Gravel’s relationship to Rocky Flats Alluvium deposition and abandonment over the period of 1.4 Ma-400 ka. We will visit younger middle Pleistocene proxies along Clear Creek showing post-Rocky Flats abandonment and incision along Clear Creek and the South Platte River during 250-70 ka. We will also visit and discuss geomorphic relationships between the ~1.4 Ma glacial deposits and 22 ka Last Glacial Maximum deposits, as defined by contemporary rock glacier modeling and paleoclimate temperature studies. Additionally, we will discuss the genesis and distribution of periglacial features, and extent of permafrost across the Denver-Front Range-Great Plains region, including nivation at Mount Morrison and periglacial erosion of the spectacular Red Rocks Amphitheatre. The field trip aims to balance contemporary geochronology and geomorphic modeling with classic geologic mapping and observation, as well as addressing unresolved geomorphic issues in the region highlighted by work in the last two decades.

title: Lead in the Environment: Geochemistry, Sources, and Remediation
chairs: Sarah M Hayes, Charles N Alpers, Tyler D Sowers | Office of Superfund and Emergency Management, Daniel Brabander | Wellesley College, Robert A Root | Department of Environmental Science
description: Join us to explore the fundamental lead (Pb) geochemistry (crystal chemistry, paragenesis, thermodynamics), human health impacts of Pb, approaches to study Pb (Pb isotopes, X-ray techniques, bioaccessibility/bioavailability assays, community engagement), and remediation of lead in the environment. We will also cover a variety of modern and legacy sources of Pb to the environment in detail. There will be participation tracks appropriate for both professional researchers and Pb-interested non-scientists to learn more about Pb, develop fundable ideas and build their network. We invite researchers, students, regulators, industry professionals, members of lead-impacted communities, and those working to reduce Pb exposure.

title: Exploring Cryogenian Snowball Earth deposits along the Colorado Front Range
chairs: Christine Siddoway, Liam Courtney-Davies Rebecca Flowers, Anthony Fuentes
description: This 1.5-day field trip will visit the enigmatic Cryogenian (720–635 Ma) Tavakaiv sandstones along the beautiful Colorado Front Range, at locations just 45 to 90 minutes from the Denver Convention Center. The unusual sandstones provide a rare, terrestrial (on-continent) record of Snowball Earth conditions, occurring as sedimentary dikes hosted by Proterozoic basement rocks and non-stratified siliciclastics forming elongate ridges. Much of the preserved Snowball Earth record elsewhere formed within shallow marine environments, whereas this trip offers a glimpse into on-land glacial processes occurring within Neoproterozoic Rodinia. Trip leaders will review a decade of work that points to a subglacial environment for sediment injection and the effects of active faults that acted as conduits for geothermal heat and mineralizing fluids. Field stops will present a range of accessible examples, including two dikes emplaced into bedrock immediately underlying the Great Unconformity erosional surface at Perry Park, a swarm of ½-m-wide to several-m wide dikes and a sandstone ridge at Buffalo Creek, and a recently discovered >50-m-long dike in Boulder Canyon. Participants will learn about a novel suite of approaches being used to determine and refine the age, sedimentation processes, and paleolatitude of the dikes and ridges when Colorado was covered by thick ice sheets during the Cryogenian, as well as how these and other data help constrain the timing of erosion at the spatially associated Great Unconformity. We encourage participants interested in modern and ancient glacial processes, sedimentology, tectonics and deep time geo-thermochronology to attend.

title: 3D numerical modeling of poly-phase sedimentary basins in Matlab: Evaluating subsidence, heat flow, and thermal histories of tectonic basins.
chairs: Magdalena Ellis Curry | Department of Marine, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences, Sarah Gelman | Department of Marine, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences, Teddie Hall | Department of Statistics, Lingxiao Gong | Department of Marine, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences
description: This short course will introduce students to a 3D numerical modeling framework developed in Matlab to investigate vertical movements and heat flow in complex poly-phase basins. Using the Arctic Alaska basin as a case study, participants will learn to integrate 1D well data and 3D depth grids to constrain models involving depth-dependent extension, flexural isostasy, and backstripping. The course covers calibrating thermal histories against %Ro and AFT datasets. Attendees will also evaluate results sensitivity and uncertainty using Monte Carlo and Neighborhood Algorithm approaches.

title: The Laramie Anorthosite Complex and Sherman Batholith: Enigmatic Magmatism and Mineralization in the Mesoproterozoic, Southern Wyoming
chairs: Madeline Lewis, Ron Frost Carol Frost
description: For over a century, geologists have debated how rocks composed of >90% plagioclase develop to form massif-type anorthosites. This field trip examines these long-standing questions using the well-exposed Mesoproterozoic Laramie Anorthosite Complex in southeastern Wyoming, one of the most accessible and well-studied anorthosite systems in the world. Participants will visit exposures of the anorthosites and associated intrusions, including monzonitic plutons and the Sherman batholith ferroan granite. The trip draws on decades of field, geochemical, and geochronologic work, including recent synthesis from a forthcoming GSA memoir led by Ron Frost. We will also consider economic geology impacts of the complex through visits to critical mineral deposits, including the Red Mountain pluton rare earth element deposit. The trip is intended for participant backgrounds, including students, early-career scientists, and experienced researchers. The trip will be based out of Laramie, WY, and include round-trip travel to Denver. We will begin with an afternoon pickup in Denver, stop at the Virginia Dale ring complex (time permitting), and travel to Laramie. The following day focuses on exposures of anorthosite intrusions in Sybille Canyon, where we will examine multiple anorthosite units and associated critical mineral deposits. The final day highlights the Sherman batholith before returning to Denver in the early evening.

title: Scientific Ocean Drilling: Where the #$*&! Is the Actual Data and How to Use It
chairs: Beth A Christensen | Department of Environmental Science, Laurel B Childress | Gulf Coast Repository
description: Over the past 50+ years of scientific ocean drilling (DSDP, ODP, IODP) a vast array of physical, chemical, and magnetic properties data, digital images, and descriptive information. has been collected during expeditions. Not only is this data an invaluable standalone resource, but it also provides the scaffolding for additional research on the cores. This workshop will teach participants how to locate scientific ocean drilling data, and provide examples of how to understand and use this data for future research.

title: Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument: Geoheritage, History, and Paleontology
chairs: Herbert Meyer Thomas Casadevall, Gabriella Harris
description: The Florissant fossil beds are world-renowned for delicate plant and insect fossils and huge petrified redwood stumps. This field trip to Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument will examine the remnants of a late Eocene landscape that includes an ash-flow tuff, lahars, and volcaniclastic lake sediments that preserve nearly 2,000 species of fossils. The dynamic history of Florissant combines many aspects that define geologic heritage, including not only Earth history but also its relation to generations of people who have used this landscape for subsistence, fossil collecting, education, commercial tourism, environmental activism, and economic development. Discussions will provide an overview of the Monument’s geoheritage and history from the early geologists and paleontologists, to the homesteaders who collected the first fossils for science, through the decades of commercial operation of two rival “petrified forest” concessions, to the establishment and operation of the national monument. The prolific scientific history of Florissant’s study extends back 150 years, beginning with the Hayden Survey. The establishment of the Monument involved a lively legal battle in 1969, which set new precedents for protection of the nation’s geoheritage during the infancy of environmental law. The scientific significance of Florissant’s geology and paleontology will be emphasized to illustrate how research is a focal point of the Monument’s mission. Highlights of the trip will include a tour of the paleontology collections and exhibit hall in the visitor center, a two-mile walk through the historic petrified forest area and along the geologic trail, and fossil collecting at a privately-owned fossil quarry.

title: Tracks, Trails, and Traces: An Accessible Introduction to Dinosaur Ridge and the Paleontological History of Denver
chairs: Ian Castro Taormina Lepore, Nancy Riggs, Christopher Atchison
description: This accessibly-designed field trip will focus on the geological and paleontological history of the greater Denver area. The trip will begin at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science, to review the geologic history of the area and gain insights regarding the ancient life that may have been present during the formation of the front range. From there, the trip will move to Dinosaur Ridge National Natural Landmark, a field setting containing both Jurassic and Cretaceous period sediments, landforms, and a large exposure of dinosaur trackways. Participants will make observations of the stratigraphy and related structures, evidence of body and trace fossils, and other geologic features along the trails. The entire group will work collaboratively and share multiple perspectives within a universally-designed inclusive community of teaching and learning. This trip is sponsored by the International Association for Geoscience Diversity (theIAGD.org), and is offered at no cost to participants. All field trip locations are wheelchair accessible and other accommodations, such as ASL interpreters, will be provided upon request.

title: AASG Geologic Mapping Field Techniques Exchange
chairs: William Andrews | Nevada Bureau of Mines and Geology, Joanna Redwine | Colorado Geological Survey, Adam Ianno | Pennsylvania Geological Survey, Katie Luciano | South Carolina Geological Survey, Stefan Kirby | Utah Geological Survey
description: This field-based short course will provide an opportunity for professional geologic mappers from diverse backgrounds and terranes to share and exchange data-collection techniques such as outcrop characterization, structural observation, lithologic description, and data-recording methods including digital field tools. This one-day field course will visit a variety of diverse outcrops in the Denver area; discussion and open exchange will be encouraged. Open to all experience levels.

title: A Bike Tour: Geology, Geochronology, and Geochemistry of the Table Mountain Shoshonite, Golden, Colorado
chairs: Leah Morgan, Lexie Millikin
description: Participants will investigate the Table Mountain lava flows by riding e-bikes around Golden, Colorado, and hiking up North Table Mountain. The Table Mountain lava flows form distinctive geographic features in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains. The lava flows are classified as shoshonites, which are potassium-rich basalts. We will explore the geology, 40Ar/39Ar geochronology, and geochemistry of shoshonite lava flows and intrusive units on North Table Mountain. The four main lava flows were extruded across the K-Pg boundary and are interbedded with the conglomeratic Denver Formation, while an intriguing intrusive unit found atop North Table Mountain is nearly 20 Ma younger but compositionally has only minor differences. We will also discuss a proposed petrogenetic model for the lava flows, their intrusive source, and relation to Laramide tectonism and the Front Range-bounding Golden fault zone. The trip will meet in downtown Golden and will involve under 10 miles of e-biking with about 550’ of elevation change (starting elevation of 5700’), as well as about 2 miles of hiking with about 500’ of elevation change.

title: Kirk Bryan Field Trip: Drying streams, beaver dams, and dam removal: Changing streamflow and sediment dynamics in rivers of the southern Colorado Rockies
chairs: Charles Shobe Katherine Lininger, Sara Warix
description: How will changes in precipitation quantity, phase, and timing affect streamflow and water storage in riparian corridors? How quickly does sediment accumulate behind beaver dams, and how much sediment can be stored behind beaver dams relative to human-built dams? How will shifting attitudes towards beavers, dam building, and dam removal change how water and sediment move through rivers? The 2026 Kirk Bryan field trip will focus on how changing environmental and management regimes affect streamflow and sediment dynamics in the rivers of the southern Colorado Rocky Mountains. This single-day trip will first stop at Manitou Experimental Forest, an intensively studied landscape situated atop the Pikes Peak batholith. We will get participants oriented to the unique geology and hydrology of this granitic landscape and then discuss recent advances from field studies of groundwater/surface water interactions and implications for future headwater streamflow. We will then stop alongside nearby Trout Creek to investigate an extensive complex of active and abandoned beaver ponds and discuss recent work quantifying beaver-driven water and sediment storage in mountain rivers as well as how beaver-driven storage compares to storage behind human-built dams. Finally, we will drive into the mouth of Elevenmile Canyon, a bedrock gorge carved by the South Platte River, to assess geomorphic and ecological responses to a recent dam removal and river restoration project. This trip is intended to foster discussion, debate, and networking among participants interested in how river corridors respond to changes in environmental boundary conditions and management practices.

title: P2. From Deep Earth to Digital Twins: Artificial Intelligence in Earth System Science and Predictive Subsurface Systems
chairs: Prosun Bhattacharya, Abhijit Mukherjee, Benjamin Jay Rostron, Courtney Killian
description: Artificial intelligence and digital twins are transforming subsurface science within Earth system frameworks. This Pardee integrates deep Earth processes, Critical Zone dynamics, groundwater systems, and critical element pathways to advance predictive modeling and decision-relevant forecasting.

title: P3. Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part I)
chairs: Priscilla Croswell Grew | Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Jack Matthews | The National Forest Company, Maria da Glória Motta Garcia | Instituto de Geociências, Ester Sztein | Director of International Programs, Steven Semken | School of Earth and Space Exploration, Sherene Andrea James-Williamson

description: This symposium focuses on the metal and mineral supply challenges of modern society and the balance between our need for metals and minerals and the societal and environmental challenges of mining.

title: 2026 Michel T. Halbouty Distinguished Lecture
description: "Geologists in the Critical Zone...in a Critical Time" The critical zone, sometimes referred to as "Living Skin of the Earth," is the ​environment where rock, soil, water, air, and living organisms interact and shape the Earth's surface. Like the human body, perhaps the Critical Zone is Earth's "largest organ." It is in humanity's best interest for all geologists, regardless of specialty, become aware of, become invested in, and communicate about, the importance of abiotic (geological) resources and processes in the critical zone. Too often one can see neglect and ignorance (dismissal) of the geological foundation when ecological conversations arise. Now more than ever, geologists need to champion our science and its importance to the viability of the Critical Zone...something NONE of us can live without.

title: GSA Presidential Address and Awards Ceremony | Glenn Thackray: The Many Paths of Geoscientists
description: The Many Paths of Geoscientists Address by GSA President Glenn Thackray Denver and the Rocky Mountain Front region have long supported a concentrated geoscience community, making this is an excellent setting in which to consider the current and future evolution of geoscience career pathways. Rapid changes in federal science focus and resource industries in recent years have caused grave concern for the future of geosciences employment. Yet, geoscience employment has long been both challenging and adaptable, clearly evolving over time as resource needs and societal attention shift. This presentation will examine the many paths that geoscientists follow and the ways in which the field in general and organizations like GSA in particular can support that evolution. At Connects 2026, GSA celebrates transition, dissolving borders, and reaching for the stars. Presenters Anke Friedrich, GSA President-elect Bridgette Moore, GSA Executive Director and CEO (Interim) Sean O’Brien, GSA Foundation Executive Director Join us as we honor individuals whose contributions have advanced the geosciences. This is more than a ceremony—it’s a celebration of vision, achievement, and community. Celebrate GSA Awardees Applaud the newly elected Society Fellows Recognize Division Primary Awardees and more

description: Professor Tobias Flore, Dr. Jeanne Lambert Sumrall from Fort Hays State University, and Professor Rian Kerrane from the University of Colorado – Denver will be leading an iron pour at this year’s GSA conference. Leading up to the iron pour a scratch-block workshop will be available for a small fee for conference participants, which allows them to make their own mold. A table will be set up all day Sunday through noon on Monday in the entrance to the convention center for mold making. This will be a first come first serve event. All the molds will be poured from 6pm – 9pm on Monday October 12 th at the University of Colorado – Denver campus using a blast furnace or what is often referred to as a coke fired cupola. Molten iron will be poured at 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,482 degrees Celsius). Faculty and students from Fort Hays state University along with faculty and staff from the University of Colorado – Denver will work with a select group of GSA conference participants to fill the molds. There will also be some molten iron performances on Monday night which you will not want to miss! Finished castings from the scratch block workshop can be picked up at the pour site Monday night or at the Karst booth Tuesday.Located outside the University of Colorado Denver and Metro State’s Shared Sculpture Studio building (1/2 mile from convention center; map will be provided at Scratch Block making table)

title: Career Fair
description: Whether you're seeking your first internship, exploring a career transition, recruiting top talent, or looking to expand your professional network, the Career Fair is designed for geoscientists at every career stage.This event brings together employers, organizations, academic institutions, government agencies, and industry professionals to connect with students, early-career professionals, mid-career specialists, and experienced leaders. Participants will have the opportunity to learn about current job openings, future hiring needs, internships, graduate programs, volunteer opportunities, and emerging career pathways across the geosciences and related fields.The Career Fair is not limited to active recruiting. Many organizations attend to share information about their work, build relationships with potential future employees, and provide insight into the skills and experiences needed for success in their sectors.Whether you're looking for your next opportunity or simply exploring what's possible, the Career Fair offers a welcoming environment to make connections, ask questions, and discover where a career in the geosciences can take you.Who should attend? chairs: Rachel Phillips, Cate Larsen, Bryan Castillo, Cameron Fetter, Luisa Hendry
description: Presenters: Rachel Phillips and Luisa Hendry Description: Join online geoscience communicators, Rachel Phillips (@GeoGirl) and Luisa Hendry (@ScottishGeologist), to learn best practices in communicating geoscience to the general public through social media. This workshop will include interactive components during which you will practice communicating your own research/expertise, as well as discussion portions focused on the importance of geoscience communication for professional development, career growth, and addressing the biggest issues facing geoscience today, such as the spread of misinformation in the media and public mistrust in science.

title: Explaining Anthropogenic Climate Change to the Public
chairs: Daniel J. Soeder
description: Presenter:Daniel J. SoederDescription:The mainstream public is experiencing the predicted effects of anthropogenic climate change. Climate denial from the fossil fuel industry and falsehoods repeated by those with political agendas have left people confused by contradictory messages. The intended audience for this session is Earth scientists who are often asked about climate change and may struggle to explain it. On a basic level, the concepts behind anthropogenic climate change are not complicated. We understand the problem and know what needs to be done to stabilize the climate. Support from a well-informed public is required.

title: Input without Advocacy: Scientific Refereeing in Public Arenas
chairs: Lauren Haygood, Todd Halihan
description: Presenters: Lauren Haygood, Todd Halihan Description:Scientists have a critical role in society by connecting policymakers, stakeholders, and the general public around societally relevant issues. This short course introduces scientific refereeing as a framework for contributing authoritative, policy-relevant science while maintaining professional neutrality and credibility. Participants will explore distinctions among refereeing, advocacy, and expertise; examine ethical and practical challenges; and practice communication strategies to clearly convey evidence, uncertainty, and scientific agreement without promoting specific policy outcomes. Through discussion and scenario-based exercises, this course equips scientists to engage effectively with policy and public audiences while preserving scientific integrity and public trust.

title: Lessons from 4 Years of 'Tree Time': Building Your Own Science Outreach Activity
chairs: Owen Madsen, Cody Kirkpatrick
description: Presenters: Owen Madsen, Cody Kirkpatrick Description: Science outreach is a great opportunity for geoscientists to connect their research to local communities, practice communication skills, and introduce the next generation of students to developing interesting science disciplines. ‘Tree Time’ is an outreach activity that explores geologic applications of dendrochronology at Indiana University’s Science Fest. This short course focuses on key lessons learned from leading and iterating four successive years of ‘Tree Time’. It aims to provide structure and guidance for participants through group activities and collaboration to make a science outreach activity catered to their research specialties.

chairs: Nancy Riggs, Robinson Cecil

title: What Do You Do When You're Stuck? From Writer's Block to Research Roadblocks—Practical Ideas for Graduate Students
description: Moderator: Ester Sztein Description: Graduate school is rarely a straight line. Whether you're facing a research dead-end, a difficult dynamic with your advisor, or the unique challenges of navigating academia as an international student, feeling stuck is a near-universal experience—but it doesn't have to be a permanent one. This panel brings together diverse voices to share hard-won strategies for pushing through stalled research, writing your thesis or dissertation when you hit the inevitable snags, building productive mentor relationships, and finding your footing when the academic environment feels overwhelming. Come ready to listen, ask questions, and leave with concrete tools you can put to work immediately. No matter where you are in your graduate journey, this session is for you.Panelists: Dr. Joshua Martin (GSA Congressional Science Fellow), Dr. Rachael Sexton (National Institute of Standards and Technology), Dr. Rolfe Mandel (University of Kansas)

description: Join us for an informal gathering that begins with inspiring remarks from leading women in geology, who will speak to the challenges and opportunities women face in the field. A relaxed networking session will follow, offering a chance to exchange ideas and connect with fellow women geoscientists. Light refreshments will be provided.

title: Workshop: How to Share Your Science and Craft Outreach Activities that Inspire Others
chairs: Luke Howard, Lilja Balaji, Margaret Yacobucci
description: Presenters: Luke Howard, Lilja Balaji, Dr. Margaret Yacobucci Description: Interested in geoscience outreach but not sure where to start? Join us for this workshop designed to help early career scientists (students, postdoctoral scholars, and others) understand the factors that shape effective science outreach and develop strategies for designing their own outreach programs. Participants in this session will: 1) explore both standard and perhaps surprising forms of outreach, 2) actively practice science communication skills with diverse audiences, and 3) discuss their own outreach experiences and activity ideas with peers and experts. At the end of the session, participants will leave with a portfolio of sample outreach activities and guides.

title: Your Guide to GSA Research Grant Programs: Undergraduate and Graduate

This session will outline the application process and eligibility criteria, and provide tips for strengthening your proposal, while also highlighting the impact of these grants on student research. A panel of past recipients will share their experiences and advice, followed by a Q&A where you can ask questions and gain insight into making the most of these opportunities.

title: Field trip dedicated to the life and contributions of Dr. Martin Lockley to understanding Front Range Geology and Paleontology: Selected Special Metropolitan Denver, Colorado area World Class Geologic Heritage Sites
chairs: Tim Connors
description: This trip will visit a selected suite of world class Geologic Heritage sites easily viewable in a single day field trip including: Red Rocks Park Amphitheatre NHL (National Historic Landmark), Morrison-Golden Fossil Areas NNL (National Natural Landmarks (aka. Dinosaur Ridge, Fossil Trace Golf Course / Triceratops Trail), Jurassic Morrison Formation type section, Interstate 70 Roadcut, Table Mountain Lava Flows, and Uranium roll front (Colorado Highway 470 & US 285). Dr. Martin Lockley was instrumental in the elevation of the Morrison Fossil Area NNL to add other sites and to expand to the Morrison-Golden Fossil Areas NNL in 2011. Field guides will be supplied, as well as numerous online resources related to each of the visited sites. Local NPS, USGS and academic geologists will “tag-team” to discuss the viewed geologic features, issues and processes. Rocks, fossils, mineral deposits, landforms, and structural features of varying ages from Precambrian to Cenozoic are present from the “Great Unconformity” of Precambrian rocks overlain by Pennsylvanian Fountain Formation at Red Rocks Park; to great sections of Paleozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic rocks of variable types and structural orientations. As part of the stop involving Dinosaur Ridge, there will be a visit to the “Martin G. Lockley Discovery Center” to view the “Deep Time Detour” exhibits and building that are a living tribute to his legacy in promoting geologic and paleontologic heritage in Colorado’s Front Range for whom this field trip is dedicated. This trip will have sponsorship from the Friends of Dinosaur Ridge and Colorado Scientific Society.

Cache la Poudre River Heritage Tour: From Historic Waterworks to Modern Innovation
chairs: Sabrina Stoker
description: Join us for a captivating field trip exploring the vital role of waterworks in our environment. We’ll visit the historic 1883 Waterworks in Fort Collins and the Bellvue Hydraulic Lab to learn about the Parshall Flume and water management. Enjoy the natural beauty of Watson Lake and its fish ladder before having lunch at New Belgium Brewing, where a presentation on the Terry Bison Ranch Project will be held. Don’t miss this opportunity to understand the essentials that sustain our communities and industries. 8 a.m.: Leave Denver 9:15 am 1883 Waterwork Works (Fort Collins first public works project) 10:30 a.m.: Bellvue Hydraulic Lab (The site where the Parshall Flume was designed to accurately measure stream flow- here we discuss irrigation, ditches, water law, and water appropriation. Could skip 1883 Waterworks and spend 2 hours here.) 11:30 a.m.: Watson Lake (Right next door to the Bellvue Hydraulic Lab. Can explore fish ladder and fish habitat.) 12:30 p.m.: New Belgium Brewing (Great spot to bring in lunch and experience an industry that relies on our healthy working river. They have a community room in which we could bring in a speaker to discuss the Terry Bison Ranch Project - the future of water supply.) 2 p.m.: Head back to Denver Registration includes ground transportation, entry fees, lunch, snacks, and water. Cost includes ground transportation, lunch, snacks, and water.

title: The Landscape Is the Classroom: Rethinking Geoscience Field Education in Iceland
description: Iceland offers an extraordinary setting for geoscience education, but the real opportunity goes beyond visiting spectacular geological sites. This presentation explores how GeoCamp Iceland uses active landscapes, local communities, natural hazards, energy systems, and UNESCO Global Geoparks as immersive learning environments. Arnbjörn Ólafsson - CEO of GeoCamp Iceland - will share practical approaches for turning field excursions into inquiry-driven learning experiences that connect geology with climate, energy, resilience, sustainability, and society. Drawing on GeoCamp Iceland’s work with students, educators, universities, and international partners, the presentation will explore how field education can create deeper connections between geoscience, place, and people, while also introducing GeoCamp’s collaboration with the Geological Society of America and upcoming GSA field experiences in Iceland.
room: Front of Exhibit Hall, CCC, Hall A

title: Understanding the Legal Landscape for Scientific Research and Advocacy
description: This presentation will discuss the legal landscape for scientists and their research. We will review the major trends in attacks on science and some of the rights and legal defenses that apply to scientists. This will include a brief overview of freedom of speech, academic freedom, and open records requests. We will also lay out best practices for scientists looking to protect themselves, their research, or their advocacy.
room: Front of Exhibit Hall, CCC, Hall A

title: Rockin' with the Brunton Axis at Field Camp

title: What Research Support Can Make Possible
description: Hear how a GSA grant became more than financial support, opening doors for research, professional growth, new connections, and opportunities. Explore how investing in emerging geoscientists can create impacts that extend well beyond a single project.

title: From Research to Bookshelf: Bringing Science to the Public
description: How do scientists turn complex research into stories that engage a broader audience? Join authors Amy Atwater (The Fossil Keeper's Treasure), Paul Bierman (When the Ice is Gone), David Montgomery (RenGen), and Rob Thomas (Montana Rocks!) for a lively conversation about bringing science beyond academia and into books for the public. Moderated by Rachel Phillips (GeoGirl), the panel will explore the challenges of writing for different audiences, finding the balance between accessibility and accuracy, and why effective science communication matters to the future of geoscience. A book signing with the authors will follow the discussion.
room: Front of Exhibit Hall, CCC, Hall A

title: The Ocean on the Top of Our Mountain: Inspiring the Next Generation of Geoscientists
description: Inspiring the next generation of geoscientists starts long before college. Using his animated film The Ocean on the Top of Our Mountain as an example, Nigel Hughes explores how animation and visual storytelling can transform complex geoscience into engaging, accessible stories, and open new possibilities for communicating science across cultures, generations, and disciplines.

title: Impact of GSA James B Thompson Lectureship: What Happens When Geoscience Travels?
description: Drawing on experiences from international Thompson Lecture tours, explore how taking science beyond familiar institutions can spark unexpected connections, exchange ideas across cultures, and create lasting opportunities for both the lecturer and host communities.

title: GSA Geoscience Policy Programs and Entities
description: This talk will describe the 4 GSA policy programs and entities: DC Policy Office (since 2007), Geology & Public Policy Committee (since 1971), Geology & Society Division (since 2003), GSA-USGS Congressional Science Fellowship (since 1986), their missions and activities, and where to find out about them on the GSA website and in other communications.

title: GSA/CampGeo Audiobook Demonstration
description: Discover a new way to explore Colorado geology! Join Jesse Reimink, creator of the CampGeo app, for a live demonstration featuring GSA’s two new e-books, Colorado Rocks! and Roadside Geology of Colorado. Learn how CampGeo brings these popular geologic guides into an interactive digital format, making it easier to discover the stories behind Colorado’s rocks and landscapes while exploring them in the field. See the app in action, hear how the new e-books can enhance your next geologic adventure, and learn more about this collaboration between GSA and CampGeo.
room: Front of Exhibit Hall, CCC, Hall A

title: From Geoscientist to Science Communicator: Building Science Communication into a Geoscience Career
description: Join this group of geoscientists and science communicators (Terri Cook, Jesse Reimink, Luisa Hendry, Jess Scanlan, Rachel Phillips) for a candid discussion about the many ways science communication can fit into a geoscience career; from institutional communications and academia to independent content creation and full-time sci comm. Panelists will share their own career paths, the opportunities and challenges of communicating science professionally, and practical advice for geoscientists looking to make science communication a bigger part of their careers.

title: Dynamic Topography: Linking Surface Records to the Evolution of the Lithosphere and Convecting Mantle
description: Explore how mantle convection, lithospheric processes, and surface evolution interact to produce dynamic topography. This talk will highlight interdisciplinary approaches that integrate geological observations, landscape and sedimentary records, and geodynamic models to better quantify vertical motions of Earth’s surface through time.

title: Geology Without Borders: Standardizing the Nation’s Maps with GeMS and ArcGIS
description: Learn how the USGS National Cooperative Geologic Mapping Program brings together geologic data from across the nation by creating a common framework for organizing and standardizing the data. This presentation highlights some of the tools and platforms that help transform these diverse datasets into a more consistent, connected view of the Nation’s geology.
